chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurara, from Humran, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah or Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man upon whom the Hadd (penalty) was established in the world, would he be punished in the Hereafter? So he said: Allah is more benevolent than that.

key_terms.أَكْرَمُ: Akram: More generous/benevolent, referring to Allah's attribute of generosity
key_terms.الدُّنْيَا: Dunya: The worldly life, as opposed to the Hereafter
key_terms.الْآخِرَةِ: Al-Akhira: The Hereafter, the life after death
key_terms.الْحَدُّ: Hadd: Prescribed punishment in Islamic jurisprudence for specific crimes

ai.seo_question: Does receiving Hadd punishment in this world exempt one from punishment in the Hereafter?
ai.summary: In this concise narration from al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (or al-Baqir) responds to a query about whether receiving the prescribed earthly punishment (Hadd) exempts a sinner from Hereafter punishment, declaring that Allah is 'more generous' (Akram) than to punish twice for the same offense. This reflects the Shia theological principle of divine magnanimity, where the physical expiation in this world is often viewed as sufficient to ward off the spiritual penalty in the next, emphasizing God's mercy over strict retribution. The brevity of the answer underscores the immediacy of divine grace in the Shia tradition, contrasting with more complex juristic debates on the sufficiency of Hadd versus general forgiveness.
